subsystems.name: Photon source
subsystems.role: produces the faint light pulses that carry each key bit — usually a laser attenuated to well below one photon per pulse, or an entangled-photon source.

subsystems.name: Encoding stage
subsystems.role: imprints each random bit on a quantum property of the photon that cannot be copied without disturbing it.
parts: random-number generator to choose the bit and the basis

subsystems.name: Quantum channel
subsystems.role: carries the photons between the two parties — optical fibre underground, or a free-space/satellite link.
parts: optical amplifiers are not usable, so loss sets the range

subsystems.name: Detectors
subsystems.role: register individual photons at the far end.
parts: or superconducting nanowire detectors for higher efficiency and lower noise

subsystems.name: Classical post-processing
subsystems.role: turns noisy raw detections into a short, secret key.

subsystems.name: Key management layer
subsystems.role: stores fresh keys and hands them to encryptors and applications on demand.

buildSteps.title: Generate the photons
buildSteps.detail: A laser is pulsed and attenuated until a pulse almost never contains more than one photon, so an eavesdropper cannot split off a copy.

buildSteps.title: Encode each bit
buildSteps.detail: A quantum random-number generator picks a bit value (0 or 1) and a basis; a modulator sets the photon's polarisation, phase or time-bin accordingly.

buildSteps.title: Transmit along the channel
buildSteps.detail: Photons travel through fibre or free space. Because the no-cloning theorem forbids copying an unknown quantum state, any interception leaves detectable disturbance.

buildSteps.title: Detect and record
buildSteps.detail: The receiver independently picks a basis for each arriving photon and measures it, logging both the outcome and the basis used.

buildSteps.title: Sift the raw key
buildSteps.detail: Over an ordinary authenticated channel the two sides compare which bases they used and keep only the cases where they matched.

buildSteps.title: Correct errors and bound eavesdropping
buildSteps.detail: They estimate the error rate from a sample of bits; a rate above roughly 11% for standard BB84 means too much was intercepted and the key is discarded.

buildSteps.title: Amplify privacy
buildSteps.detail: Hashing compresses the remaining bits so that any partial information an eavesdropper holds becomes negligible, yielding a shorter secret key.

buildSteps.title: Deliver keys to the encryptors
buildSteps.detail: The key manager supplies keys to one-time-pad or AES encryptors; because the classical channel is only computationally authenticated, it is typically hardened with post-quantum algorithms too.

prerequisites.why: without efficient, low-noise detectors the key rate collapses and the range shrinks.
fibre loss caps practical links at roughly a few hundred kilometres without relays.
QKD itself provides no authentication, so an unauthenticated classical channel can be impersonated.
these would extend range beyond fibre loss limits and remove the need for trusted relay nodes.
standardised in 2024 and being deployed; it is the software-only alternative that protects data against future quantum computers without special hardware.

pathway.milestone: metro QKD links and trusted-node networks in operation, including a long intercity trunk line in China and testbeds in Europe
pathway.unlocks: proof that key distribution works over installed fibre, though at limited distance and cost.

pathway.milestone: satellite QKD and intercontinental key exchange
pathway.unlocks: key distribution between distant ground stations where no fibre exists.
longer links without trusting intermediate nodes.
security that does not rely on trusting the hardware itself.
